alignment_log.scope: Initial alignment pass for all three posts: AP CSP, California K-12 CS Standards, ISTE Digital Citizen, UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students, CASEL, VIA, AASL Engage, CA CTE (ICT) anchor standards.
alignment_log.note: Finding Fido already carried a hand-written standards table (castandards, apcsp, ISTE) in its own appendix -- those four codes are kept as-is here, just moved into this carrier's shape. Can a Company Have a Conscience and Prove Me Wrong had no prior alignment; both are read fresh against every catalog. apcsp 5.1 (Beneficial and Harmful Effects) is the one code genuinely common to all three posts -- surveillance (Fido), a company's own ethical stance (Conscience), and AI's effect on learning (Prove Me Wrong) are three different instances of the same Big Idea, so it's one coverage entry with three locators and a locator_notes override per post rather than three near-duplicate entries. CSTA 2017/2026 were checked but left out for Conscience and Prove Me Wrong -- castandards and apcsp already cover the same ground more specifically for those two, and adding CSTA on top would be padding, not new coverage. Little Brother (the novel unit) stays in its own carrier, little_brother.json -- it's a multi-week unit with its own chapter-by-chapter locators, not a single-post source like these three.

alignment_log.scope: Added the four new Socratic-seminar posts (the STUDENTS FIRST Act, the Salamanca robot tutor, the Nest doorbell camera, the Digital Education Council survey) to this carrier's existing apcsp coverage, at the same topic-level granularity (5.x, 2.x) this carrier already uses -- not the finer IOC-1.A/DAT-2.A-style essential-knowledge codes the posts themselves cite inline, since no carrier in this project cites at that grain and the coverage-map widget is built around topic-level keys.
alignment_log.note: Read each post's own Learning Goals and, where present, its own explicit "AP CSP, Big Idea 5" section (Robot Tutor and Delete both already name their topics outright; Rules Students Wrote and Who Sets the Rules do not, so their topic-level codes are derived here from the IOC-1.x/DAT-2.x essential-knowledge codes each post cites, via apcsp.json's own topic->LO mapping). 5.1 (Beneficial and Harmful Effects) extends to all four, same reasoning as the existing three-locator entry: a school-district robot, a doorbell camera's residual data, a 49-rule student bill, and a survey about unclear AI rules are four more instances of the same beneficial/harmful tension. 5.5 (Legal and Ethical Concerns) extends to Rules Students Wrote (who decides what AI use is "permitted") and Robot Tutor (the Commissioner's letter, the paused data-privacy agreement). 5.2 (Digital Divide) and 5.3 (Computing Bias) are new, Robot Tutor only -- 5.3 is marked partial, since the post's own reading and core rounds don't build bias in directly; it surfaces only as one back-pocket CS-lens question ("Could a robot tutor be biased?"), unlike 5.2's Salamanca-district framing, which the reading leads with. 5.6 (Safe Computing) is new, shared by Robot Tutor (student IDs, stored conversations, flagged-term alerts) and Delete (the whole post). 2.3 (Extracting Information from Data), also new, is Who Sets the Rules only -- its reading is explicitly "data, not a story," and paragraph 8's self-reported/college-only/no-fieldwork-dates critique is this topic's own cautions about what a dataset can and can't show, not just a beneficial/harmful framing. Deliberately did not duplicate the CASEL/VIA/UNESCO-MIL discourse-skill alignment prove-me-wrong already carries here (REL.1, RDM.2, SOC.1, COU.2, VI.A.2, 8.4) across these four posts too -- those codes describe the Socratic Seminar format itself (the fishbowl, the norms, the tickets), not any one post's content, and that format now lives in its own shared page (socratic-seminar-kit.md, linked from all seven seminar posts), so its alignment belongs once on that page's own carrier (socratic_seminar_kit) instead of copied seven times. Common Core ELA and AB 873, which every seminar post also cites, stay as the kit's own prose for the same reason this carrier already keeps AB 873 out of its coverage object: a legislative mandate and an ELA framework this catalog system doesn't model, not something to force into a coverage key.

Re-read the current post against its existing 5.1/5.6 notes -- both still hold; the content that changed (the three-company retention table, the two-video Round 2) reinforces 5.6 and the post's own documented/claimed/unknown thread rather than displacing anything. That same expanded Round 2 is new, genuine coverage, though: judging a creator's video against a competitor's parody, with the post's own text already doing some of the sorting ("Ring disputes parts of what the videos say"), is unesco-mil code 5 (Critically Evaluate Content) applied to this post's own reading, not the kit's generic discourse-skill claim -- added as a new entry rather than folded into the kit carrier, since it's specific to what this post asks students to evaluate, not the format itself.

Re-read the full current post, including the reading include (_includes/robot-reading.html) and the Round 2/3 content added since the last pass. 5.1, 5.2, 5.5, 5.6 all still hold against the current reading text, unchanged. 5.3 (Computing Bias) is upgraded from partial to strong: the original pass found only a single back-pocket question ("Could a robot tutor be biased?"); the current post has the avatar interview itself demonstrate a bias-probing exchange ("who is better at math, boys or girls") with a facilitator question that pushes past a surface-level good answer to ask how you'd actually test for bias -- real reading content now, not a hypothetical prompt. New: unesco-ai-cfs 4.2.1 (AI creators and service providers carry real legal and social obligations), for Round 3's vendor-history trust question -- a different claim from 5.5's existing data-privacy-agreement framing, about whether to believe a vendor's promises given its own corporate history. Did not add a code for "Playing the Other Side" here -- that mechanism is now a shared, every-seminar kit feature (see socratic-seminar-kit.md's own new section), so its standard (via-character WIS.3) was added to socratic_seminar_kit.json instead, not duplicated per post.

meta.caveat: A single blog post per locator, not a chaptered source -- locator_kind is "none". California Ed Code Section 33548 (AB 873/AB 2876, media literacy and AI literacy) is cited directly by Finding Fido and Prove Me Wrong, but it's a legislative mandate, not a framework in this catalog system, so it isn't represented here -- it stays as a short line of prose in each post instead. The four newest posts (students-wrote-the-rules-seminar, robot-teacher-seminar, you-deleted-it-is-it-gone, who-sets-the-rules-for-ai) are Socratic seminars built on a shared format page, socratic-seminar-kit.md, which carries its own Common Core ELA and AB 873 prose plus its own carrier (socratic_seminar_kit) for the discourse-skill standards that format itself practices -- this carrier covers only each post's own reading and content, not the shared format. you-deleted-it-is-it-gone was renamed after this carrier's first alignment pass (was what-does-delete-mean-seminar), and the robot-tutor seminar even more so (robot-teacher-seminar -> two more intermediate slugs -> can-robotic-ai-teachers-replace-human-teachers) -- if a locator ever stops matching again, check the post's own redirect_from list for its prior slugs before assuming the content changed.

5.1.note: Big Idea 5's Beneficial and Harmful Effects topic, applied seven different ways across these posts.

locator_notes.can-a-company-have-a-conscience: A company's own AI being weighed for both its military and consumer harms and benefits is this topic's dual-use framing in a single real news story.
locator_notes.finding-fido-or-finding-you: The Ring ad is a beneficial-looking feature (finding a lost dog) that doubles as harmful infrastructure (a neighborhood surveillance network) -- IOC-1's core tension, named explicitly in the post's own 'function creep' section.
locator_notes.prove-me-wrong: The seminar's central question -- when AI use helps learning versus steals the practice that builds it -- is this topic's beneficial/harmful framing applied to the tool itself, not just to society.
locator_notes.students-wrote-the-rules-seminar: Six real provisions from a 98-student-written national AI policy, including a rule that can suspend a student over a parent's AI use, are weighed for who they help and who they punish -- the post's own learning goal names IOC-1.A and IOC-1.B directly.
locator_notes.can-robotic-ai-teachers-replace-human-te: A $57,590 humanoid tutor that can also log a student's ID and conversation history is a single innovation argued as helpful (an underserved district getting new tech first) and harmful (a state pause over data-privacy concerns) in the same reading.
locator_notes.you-deleted-it-is-it-gone: The post's own learning goal states this directly: "weigh a helpful and a damaging outcome of the same design decision: keeping data a user thinks is gone" -- the FBI's recovered footage versus a camera owner's belief that pressing Delete meant gone.
locator_notes.who-sets-the-rules-for-ai: 88% of students using AI and 57% saying the rules are unclear is the same beneficial/harmful tension read through a number instead of a story -- the post's own learning goal cites IOC-1.A and IOC-1.B.

5.2.note: Salamanca is a small, high-poverty district on the Seneca Nation reservation that chose to be among the first in the country to buy a humanoid classroom robot -- the reading leads with exactly this framing, and one facilitator question asks it directly: does this narrow the gap between rich and poor schools, or widen it?

5.3.note: The avatar interview itself tests this: asked who is better at math, boys or girls, it "gives a good answer," and a facilitator question pushes past that surface pass -- "Is saying the right thing enough for a tutor? How would you test whether it is biased?" This is the reading's own content now, not a single back-pocket question standing in for the topic.

5.5.note: A company's Pentagon contract, its self-imposed ethical red lines (no mass surveillance, no autonomous weapons), and the legal/political fallout are Legal and Ethical Concerns in its most direct, current-events form.

locator_notes.students-wrote-the-rules-seminar: Rule A treats any AI use not explicitly permitted as plagiarism, and Rule B can suspend a student over a parent's AI use -- the post's second learning goal names the legal and ethical question outright: who decides what's "permitted," and who answers for it.
locator_notes.can-robotic-ai-teachers-replace-human-te: The Education Commissioner's letter and the district's pause "while it works through enhanced student data privacy agreements" are Legal and Ethical Concerns playing out as an actual, unresolved regulatory question, not a hypothetical.

5.6.note: Safe Computing's own ground -- personal data a system collects and what can go wrong keeping it.

locator_notes.can-robotic-ai-teachers-replace-human-te: Each student logs in with a unique ID the robot uses to recall past conversations, and flagged words trigger an automatic alert to administrators -- the CS-lens questions ask directly what that data is and who could see it.
locator_notes.you-deleted-it-is-it-gone: The entire reading is this topic: a camera marked disconnected, no paid subscription, and the FBI still recovering video from "residual data located in backend systems" -- the post's own Standards section names 5.6 first.

2.3.note: The reading is built to be "data, not a story": a 45,000-person, 35-country survey reduced to a few real percentages, with paragraph 8 explicitly flagging what the numbers can and can't support (self-reported, college students only, no fieldwork dates given) -- Extracting Information from Data applied to the reading itself, not just its topic.

9-12.IC.26.note: A single company's contract decision reshaping its relationship with the federal government, consumer sentiment, and a competitor's own choices in the same week is exactly this standard's 'new technologies reshape social, economic, and political structures' claim, playing out in real time.

9-12.IC.23.note: From the post's own appendix: computing's social and cultural effects, not always for the better -- the Ring ad backlash across senators, privacy groups, and ordinary users.

9-12.IC.29.note: From the post's own appendix: Search Party is on by default and opt-out, meaning most camera owners' footage gets pulled into the system without ever actively agreeing to it -- this standard's 'automatic data collection without active participation' almost verbatim.

9-12.IC.30.note: From the post's own appendix: weighing privacy against the safety and law-enforcement case Ring's founder makes for near-zero neighborhood crime is this standard's privacy-vs-safety-and-law tradeoff.

6-8.IC.20.note: The post's own appendix cites the 6-8 band more lightly than the 9-12 one (just this code, not .21 bias or .22 collaboration, neither of which the post actually covers) -- the same tradeoffs argument, pitched for a middle-school read.

6-8.IC.24.note: Grades 7-9 seminar: a default setting is a choice between two competing goods, a lost dog found fast versus neighbors' cameras searched without being asked. Students weigh it in Round 1 and state it again on the exit ticket (leave it on, or turn it off).

1.2.d.note: The post's own appendix cites ISTE 2b under an older numbering; this catalog's current Digital Citizen standard covering the same ground -- managing personal data and awareness of data-collection technology -- is 1.2.d.

4.2.1.note: "AI creators and service providers carry real legal and social obligations" is this post's whole premise: Anthropic choosing to hold a line its own leadership calls a matter of conscience, and facing real consequences for it.

locator_notes.can-a-company-have-a-conscience: "AI creators and service providers carry real legal and social obligations" is this post's whole premise: Anthropic choosing to hold a line its own leadership calls a matter of conscience, and facing real consequences for it.
locator_notes.can-robotic-ai-teachers-replace-human-te: Round 3's whole point is this standard by name: "should a vendor's history affect whether you believe its promises?" The district's entire safety case ("no access to personally identifiable student information," "closed system") is a set of promises from a vendor whose own corporate history is then put in question -- a legal/social-obligation question about the company, not just the robot.

4.3.1.note: Critically examining how AI and the companies behind it affect society, as a responsible citizen would.

locator_notes.can-a-company-have-a-conscience: The post explicitly frames the question for students as theirs to weigh, not just the company's: "Can a company have a conscience? ... I'm asking you."
locator_notes.prove-me-wrong: The whole seminar format exists to make students examine AI's role in their own learning and honesty, not just absorb a rule about it.

4.2.2.note: "Safe and responsible use" -- understanding ethical principles and when a tool helps versus harms -- is the exact question the seminar's facilitator prompts return to again and again: "when does the tool help you, and when does it steal the practice you needed?"

SA.4.note: The post's closing line, "this is how we show students that character counts," is a direct appeal to honesty and integrity as self-aware values, even though the lesson's content is a corporate ethics case study, not a personal-identity exercise.

REL.1.note: The fishbowl format -- one voice at a time, building on what came before, citing evidence -- is a structured implementation of communicating effectively, not just a discussion format left to chance.

RDM.2.note: "Cite the text or a real example when you make a claim" (one of the five posted norms) and the observer organizer's evidence columns are this standard's reasoned-judgment-from-evidence made into a gradable classroom routine.

SOC.1.note: The whole design -- inquiry first, teacher opinion held back until the reveal, a before/after temperature check scored by who changed the most minds -- exists specifically to get students taking each other's perspectives seriously, not performing a position.

COU.2.note: Honesty, in VIA's own sense of presenting yourself accurately and taking responsibility for your actions, is the lesson's explicit subject (a cheating scandal) and its own closing instruction to students: "I grade effort and honesty here, not the position landed on."

WIS.3.note: Judgment -- weighing a decision from multiple angles, including evidence that cuts against what you already believe -- is what the before/after temperature check is built to surface, though the seminar format exercises it more than it explicitly teaches it as a named skill.

VI.A.2.note: Ethical Use -- understanding what counts as ethical use of a tool before you reach for it -- is the seminar's core content: when AI use on schoolwork crosses from help into substituting for the learning itself.

8.4.note: Personal integrity and ethical behavior is this standard's workplace framing of the same academic-honesty question the seminar raises about AI use, applied to a classroom rather than a job.

5.note: Round 2 is built around judging two sources with competing interests (a creator arguing a position, a competitor running a parody ad), explicitly naming what's documented versus only claimed ("Ring disputes parts of what the videos say"), then a 'Sort It' exercise that has students do the sorting themselves -- Critically Evaluate Content as the reading's own structure, not just its topic.

2-IC-20.note: Same evidence as 6-8.IC.20 above, via the castandards-csta2017 crosswalk (strength: strong).

2-IC-23.note: Same evidence as 6-8.IC.24 above, via the castandards-csta2017 crosswalk (strength: strong). Numbering shifts: CA's IC.24 is CSTA's 2-IC-23.

3A-IC-29.note: Same evidence as 9-12.IC.29 above, via the castandards-csta2017 crosswalk (strength: strong).

MS-SOC-HI-39.note: This carrier's own inference -- no official source exists for the 2026 revision: Ring's stated purpose for Search Party (pets only) set against the founder's stated goal (reduce crime) is a technology's original purpose versus its possible effects on privacy.

MS-SOC-HU-43.note: This carrier's own inference: on by default and six steps to turn off are human decisions behind the system, and the seminar asks students to judge them.

MS-SOC-ET-42.note: This carrier's own inference: whether Search Party helps or harms a neighborhood is the debatable question the seminar asks students to argue, with evidence from the reading.

HS-SOC-HU-43.note: This carrier's own inference: the same human-decisions point for the 9th graders, who also name a rule an engineer could check.
